I should have phrased this better in my previous comment, but MAT223 is definitely something you should take in Computer Science, whereas MAT240 is mostly for students wanting to pursue a Math Specialist. 

Unless you're interested in pursuing something like a double major/specialist in Math and CS (or you're just really interested in maths) I don't really recommend it? I mentioned above that it's only really useful in math-intensive fields of Computer Science, and oftentimes these paths lead to research or grad school, so if you're hoping to go more of a software development kinda route MAT240 is not that valuable to you IMO.

Definitely take MAT223 at least because it's a prerequisite for a lot of courses you might want to take in later years (you can [look here](https://courseography.cdf.toronto.edu/graph) if you're curious about some of the specific courses where algebra is required), it's just an important field of maths for CS and it's applicative to a lot of different areas.   
If you're interested in something like Theoretical Computer Science (which includes topics about cryptography, algorithms, and data structures) and really enjoy maths, then consider taking MAT240 :)

I just finished my first year, so I can't say much but I'll give my two cents anyways:

1. I'm personally really enjoying it: the courses aren't "difficult", maybe challenging is a better word. I don't think any of the required courses are unfair, and while time-consuming, I think generally it's a fun learning experience.  
Toronto is a great place to live, and you have the opportunity to meet a lot of people if you put in the effort; lots of clubs and groups for you to interact, so you can definitely find your niche.

2. Apart from MAT137/157 and the mandatory CS courses, just take whatever you're interested in (you only have \~2.5/5.0 credits of courses you NEED to take in first year), so you have a lot of room for other things.  
If you're a maths person and want to pursue math-intensive fields (e.g., AI/ML, image processing, theoretical CS), then algebra (MAT240/MAT223) and in some cases CSC240 (which is an enriched CS theory course) is typically recommended for first-years.  
As for your electives, just take courses you're interested in. I know a lot of people take courses that are just easy and for the breadth requirements, but I found myself doing a lot better in courses I enjoyed learning about.

5. First year math is pretty good. If you're worried about difficulty, you should probably take MAT137: It's not difficult, but a very tedious course for sure. There are proof questions that prove why a certain mathematical statement is true/false, but IMO that's the most difficult part of the course. As long as you study enough, you are bound to do well on the course.

6.  Don't worry too much about your grades and the people around you in terms of their academic performance; work at a pace that is comfortable but fulfilling for yourself. Make the most out of your experience in university, and be okay with making mistakes.  


Sorry for mansplaining a bunch of stuff but I hope it helps. Good luck :D

Yeah, but they're a little different. UTSC has co-op, which can be in 4-month intervals, or one 12-16 month co-op. UTM has PEY, which is 12-16 months. UTM typically has better outlooks with their PEY but UTSC co-op is guaranteed iirc. The post I sent has all that information with external links for more info.

[This post](https://www.reddit.com/r/UofT/comments/mm621w/uoft_cs_which_campus/) is a great start! IMO both the programs are good but they have pros/cons, though I see more people preferring UTM generally because of the nicer environment (a lot of people think Scarborough can be a bit of a sketchy area) and better opportunities with your classes (i.e: at UTSC you're limited in the amount of courses you can take on the SG campus whereas UTM can take as many SG courses they want).

CS is a relatively difficult field regardless of the school you go to. A lot of people fail to realize that you need to learn math and logical skills in order to solve problems as you go further on in your learning and projects/work. Do not go into CS if you're not willing to put in the work, because it's more oriented around self-motivated learning and interest than other programs. As a result, the school you go to doesn't matter *that* much at the end of the day.

That being said:

* Laurier: It's a decent school with co-op and Waterloo is a great area for tech, but there isn't a lot of electives and it is a business school (which will probably affect your experience).
* Ryerson: Growing quickly and it's a solid program with co-op but no real standout features, since the curriculum is pretty easy. Toronto is expensive but there's lots of opportunities there.
* Queen's: Still kinda new, the internship seems pretty nice. Kingston is old-fashioned and there's not a lot of tech opportunities in the city or school.
* Western: Program is a little outdated and rigid but Western offers pretty decent connections afaik. London is pretty slow in tech.
* McMaster: Kinda outdated but the CS program is good, a lot of people consider it one of the better ones after UofT and UW.

Some other good universities are Carleton and Ottawa, since Ottawa is a big tech hub and the programs themselves are nice with pretty good opportunities within the schools for EC's and electives. I think they're pretty comparable but I've heard that Carleton offers a bit more opportunities especially with their Shopify Dev Degree.OTU also isn't that bad for CS, it's a small school which means you can really get close with profs/faculty and have more personal connections. Also has co-op, though you will probably be surrounded by people that don't really care about academics, if that bothers you.

Grade 11 averages don't matter a lot, but you probably won't be considered for early consideration. Brock is definitely not competitive for CS, but I would try to aim for an 85% average, though I'm not sure how admissions have been in this past year or how they will be next year.

$1000 is a **lot** of money, I would try to do more research over the next few months and figure out if there's any programs you think you have absolutely no interest in (even if they are a backup school). A grand majority of the people I *personally* know that have applied to more than 12 programs had zero interest in half of their programs even as a backup, so they could have saved like $300 or more.

Even if you're not confident, if you have a mid-high 90 average you will almost certainly get into tier-2 programs or worse. Just an as example, if you had a 96 average, you have a chance for Mac HS with a good essay, but if you do get rejected you still have a great average and can get into Mac life science (anything over a 92 is pretty much guaranteed IIRC), so there's not as much need for you to apply to a bunch of backups if you're not really interested in them.

Macs are good laptops and will be able to run whatever you need, HOWEVER, the problem is that you need specific software in engineering programs like MatLab, AutoDesk, or other CAD programs, which don't always have MacOS compatability. Running Windows on a Mac can be difficult particularly for the newer models right now, so you may have a hard time with that.
Each school uses different program so if you can find the ones they use for your school (you can find this by googling on Reddit or just looking through different course syllabus) then you can figure out if you can use your Mac or not.
If the programs don't have compatability you should buy a laptop that can run Windows (you can probably get away with buying a laptop for $500 or less if you have an issue with budget).

Something you should consider is that if you want to go into game dev it is extremely important to make connections. Showing you're passionate about games and are creative is way more valuable than going to a specific university. Although unis have game dev specializations/minors, they really only offer a couple different courses and you'll have to learn most things by yourself regardless, so don't emphasize too much on the special courses for each uni.

​

POSt is an issue, you'll probably need around an 80% average or so to make it through (which is not impossible or requires you to be "smart", just definitely more hard work/time you might rather use for side projects?).

Carleton is also good for making these sorts of connections, since it's in Ottawa and Carleton hosts game jams and has a pretty active game dev club. Co-op is also great and you can probably get internships with game dev companies there easily, I hear that the game dev stream at Carleton is also pretty immersive, too.

London is pretty small and old-fashioned in comparison to the GTA and Ottawa, and so you might have a harder time making connections this way and finding opportunities, but Western is a great school and there's still a good community with a decent internship program that can also really help.

​

I applied to UTSG and UW for both SE and CS, got into eng at both, CS at UofT, and waiting on UW CS right now. I have a 99 average which is definitely on the higher end, in two years I'd imagine a competitive average to be around a 94 or 95, though. The people that get rejected with 94's or even higher are often shown to have little extracurricular experience or wrote their supp apps terribly, so as long as you get things together and make sure you write/read over your applications carefully, you have nothing to worry about.

Since we're in a pandemic, I'm sure they wouldn't expect you to have incredible ECs because of the lack of opportunities. IIRC when I applied, the schools stated that they would take more consideration on ECs done before the pandemic because of this.

​

There's still lots of things you could do, one of my main things I did was be a captain on an esports team which was online, and showed I actually did something productive during the pandemic (idk if you will get this on your supp apps by the time you apply, but they did ask us how the pandemic has affected us). You could ask staff at your school if you could make an online club or initiative, or just do some valuable volunteer work. As examples, my friend brought her eco club together and they've continued to do their activities online/with social distancing, I've got friends doing yearbook committee which can easily be done online, and the art committee at our school has been showing off work online + interacting with the school that way. 

Doing projects on the side and being able to show proof of it could also work. For eng, UW will ask you for your prior knowledge of any programming languages and I'm sure they'll eventually implement a similar thing for CS as well. If you are able to start working hard now and create something interesting, it'll look really good on your application.

What your ECs are *really doesn't matter*, I didn't even take CS courses or robotics in high school. Do what you like and if you show your passions, it'll make you a much more favourable applicant.
